q152: 🚂 Stage 1 — CLOCK (the bit train): The chip has eight cells. With each CLOCK pulse, the bit on the DATA wire enters from the left (Q0) and the rest move one cell to the right. Goal: set DATA to 1 and give one CLOCK so a 1 bit enters; each time you give CLOCK, that 1 moves one cell further. The bottom row (latch) does nothing for now.
q153: Set DATA to 1 and give CLOCK; watch the bit enter one cell. Then give CLOCK again to move it further.
q154: 💡 You learned: bits move only on the CLOCK pulse, and DATA is read exactly at the moment CLOCK goes high (the yellow dot in the timing diagram). 8 pulses = 8 bits; the first bit reaches Q7 and the ninth pulse pushes it out the end (in a real circuit it goes on to the next chip, which means you can chain several chips).
q156: 📌 Stage 2 — LATCH (the display case): Inside the chip there are two rows. The top row (shift) changes with every CLOCK, but the LEDs are connected to the bottom row (latch), which copies from the top row only on the LATCH pulse. Goal: send a few 1 bits into the register, see that the LEDs don't move, then give LATCH.
q157: Send bits a few times with DATA = 1 and CLOCK. Look at the LEDs: they're still off. Then give LATCH.
q158: 💡 You learned: without the latch, the LEDs would show a half-finished pattern at every shift and flicker. The latch lets you gather all 8 bits first and then show them at once. Try it: give a few more CLOCKs; the top row changes but the LEDs don't, until the next LATCH.
q160: 🎯 Stage 3 — Challenge: Light the LEDs like the “target” dots (under the LEDs). Think: which cell does the first bit you send end up in at the end? If you get stuck, the “Hint” button shows the sending order.
q161: Send 8 bits (DATA + CLOCK), then give LATCH. The target dots turn green if they're right.
q162: Well done! With every clock the bits move one step forward.
q163: Right! Latch means “show everything at once”.

q166: The 74HC595 is a “serial-to-parallel converter”: it takes bits one by one from
q170: at the same time. That means when the Arduino's pins run out, with just 3 pins (DATA, CLOCK, LATCH) you get 8 new outputs; and if you chain several chips one after another (cascading), 16, 24 and more outputs.
